summary: Tartarian honeysuckle is a shrub, usually 6 to 15 feet tall, with small, very fragrant tube-shaped flowers. It forms very dense thickets that crowd out and suppress native plants, and invasive honeysuckle berries are less fatty and nutritious than native ones, which can harm migrating birds that eat lots of them. Invasive honeysuckles have hollow stems, while native honeysuckles have solid stems.
history: Tartarian honeysuckle is native to Central Asia and southern Russia. It is believed to have been brought to North America as an ornamental as early as the 1750s. It escaped cultivation and is easily spread by birds.
seasons: It flowers from May to June with small, very fragrant tube-shaped flowers, from creamy white to shades of pink and crimson. Its quarter-inch red berries appear from mid-summer through early fall.

handling.text: Because birds spread the seeds, control should start in late summer or early fall, before the berries are ready. Seedlings and young plants can be removed by hand when there are only a few, repeated every year. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
